settings.botDelayInfo: The opponents are simulated, so they could act instantly. This holds the board for a moment on each of their turns instead, the way a real table has someone thinking before they discard — long enough to see what each seat actually threw. Set it to 0 to play at full speed.

modeHint.efficiency: Plays the most efficient discard every turn.
modeHint.defense: Folds — plays the safest tile against every seat in riichi.
modeHint.tsumogiri: Discards whatever it just drew, every turn — no hand management at all.
modeHint.ev: Pushes or folds by expected value, with every term of the arithmetic written down.
modeHint.manual: You play this seat: discards, calls and riichi are your choice.

evModelHint.statistical: Every price derived from the tiles nobody has seen. It prices opponents cheap, so it pushes where the measured model folds.
evModelHint.houou: Every price measured over Tenhou houou games. Four-player only — there is no three-player data.

evObjectiveHint.points: Maximises the score. Stable, and the currency every figure is easiest to check in.
evObjectiveHint.placement: Maximises where the match is likely to finish, so the same points are worth more to a seat with a place to gain.

abort.question: Nine orphans — {{kinds}} distinct terminals and honours.

ukeire.desc: The tiles that would improve your hand if drawn next — fewer kinds and copies mean a narrower path to tenpai. The efficiency trainer counts it after every discard.

tedashi.desc: A discard pulled from your hand rather than the tile you just drew. It reveals more about your hand than a tsumogiri does, since it shows you chose to keep the drawn tile instead.

tsumogiri.desc: Discarding the tile you just drew, untouched. It gives away less information than a tedashi, because your hand shape didn't visibly change.

shanten.desc: How many tile exchanges a hand needs to reach tenpai. 0 means already tenpai (waiting to win); -1 means already won.

genbutsu.desc: A tile provably safe against a specific riichi: it's already in that player's own discards, or someone discarded it after their riichi without being ronned. The only tier that's actually 100% safe.

furiten.desc: A tenpai seat that can't ron at all right now: one of its own waits is sitting in its own discards, or it passed up a winning tile earlier this hand. It can still tsumo — only the ron is blocked.

suji.desc: A tile whose matching ryanmen (two-sided wait) is ruled out because its genbutsu counterpart three away is already safe (e.g. 4 is suji if 1 is genbutsu). It only rules out that one wait shape — tanki, shanpon and kanchan waits on the same tile are untouched.

dora.desc: A bonus-value tile indicated by the dora indicator (the next tile after it in sequence). It adds to a hand's han but is not itself a yaku — a hand needs a real yaku to win even with dora.

uraDora.desc: A second, hidden dora indicator revealed only for hands that win by riichi. It rewards riichi specifically, on top of whatever yaku and dora the hand already has.

home.title: Riichi Trainer
home.license: Free and open-source software, released under the GPLv3.

efficiency.title: Efficiency trainer - with opponents
efficiency.desc: Pick the best discard against real opponents at a full table.
efficiency.intro:
What it is: one full hand of mahjong, from the deal onward. You play one seat and the other seats draw, discard and call for themselves, so tiles leave the wall the way they do in a real game.

Why it matters: the hand that reaches tenpai first usually wins it, and every discard either keeps ways of getting there or throws them away. This one choice decides more hands than scoring or defence ever will.

How to play: on each of your turns, discard the tile that leaves your hand closest to tenpai and with the most tiles still able to improve it — that count is its ukeire. The trainer then names the best discard and how many improving tiles yours cost you. Reaching tenpai ends the hand, and a new one is dealt from there.

efficiencySolo.title: Efficiency trainer - solo
efficiencySolo.desc: Draw and discard your way to tenpai alone.
efficiencySolo.intro:
What it is: the same discard choice as the trainer with opponents, with the table taken away. You are dealt thirteen tiles and draw from a full wall by yourself — nobody else discards, calls or wins — so a hand simply runs from the deal until you reach tenpai.

Why it matters: with no opponents to read and no calls to fear, every decision is only about the shape of your own hand. That is tile efficiency on its own, and it is the skill the table trainers are built on top of.

How to play: draw, then discard the tile that leaves your hand closest to tenpai and with the most tiles still able to improve it — that count is its ukeire. The trainer names the best discard and how many improving tiles yours cost you.

shanten.title: Shanten trainer
shanten.desc: Guess how far a hand is from tenpai.
shanten.intro:
What it is: a hand appears and you say its shanten — how many tile exchanges it still needs to reach tenpai. 0 means it is already tenpai and waiting to win, 1 means one useful swap away, and so on.

Why it matters: shanten is the number every discard is measured against, since "which tile is better" almost always means "which one keeps shanten lower". Reading it at a glance is what makes the rest of the game fast.

How to play: the hand is up and the clock is already running, so answer with the buttons (or type the number) and the next hand is dealt straight away, the previous answer kept beside it. Pause stops the clock; reset hides the hand and deals a fresh one, since a hand you have already studied cannot be timed again.

scoring.title: Scoring trainer
scoring.desc: Guess han, fu and points for a winning hand.
scoring.intro:
What it is: a completed winning hand, shown with everything its value depends on — the round and seat winds, the dora indicators, whether it was won by ron or tsumo, riichi and the rest.

Why it matters: what a hand is worth is what tells you whether it is worth pushing for, and at a real table the winner is expected to count it themselves. It is also the one part of the game you can practise entirely away from the table.

How to play: work out the yaku, add up the han and fu, and enter the points before checking the answer. Settings choose which of the three you are asked for, and can switch on the full yaku and fu breakdowns once you want to see where each number came from.

folding.title: Folding trainer
folding.desc: Someone declared riichi. Pick the safest tile to throw.
folding.intro:
What it is: an opponent has declared riichi and your own hand is not worth pushing. The board is handed to you a turn or two later, and from then until the hand ends you pick the tile least likely to deal into them.

Why it matters: dealing in is the single biggest way to lose points, and hands you cannot win are common. Folding well protects more points across a game than a few extra wins add.

How to play: judge from public information only — tiles they discarded themselves (genbutsu, which they can never win on), tiles thrown since their riichi without being claimed, suji, and shapes the visible tiles already rule out. What they actually hold never counts against you: a tile from the safest tier is graded correct even when it turns out to be in their wait.

lab.title: Statistical lab
lab.desc: Load or build any hand and see the full ranking — every discard's shanten and ukeire, every tile's danger tier.
lab.intro: Load a shared wall or build your own hand, tile by tile. Play only your own discards — opponents always play themselves. Nothing is graded: every discard's full ukeire ranking and every tile's full danger-tier breakdown are shown, the same numbers the other trainers compute and only show you a sliver of.

match.title: Full match
match.desc: Play a whole east-only or hanchan match against the bots — nothing graded, just the game.
match.intro: Pick a format and a ruleset, choose who plays each seat, then play the match out round by round — dealer rotation, honba, riichi sticks and all. Nothing here is graded: the points are the score.

reason.halfSuji: only one side is suji — the ryanmen on the other side is still live
reason.nonSuji: nothing on the table rules it out
